+
+##################################################################
+
+$code=".text\n";
+
+if ($avx512vaes) {
+
+$code.=<<___;
+.extern  OPENSSL_ia32cap_P
+
+#################################################################
+# Signature:
+#
+# int ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible(void);
+#
+# Detects if the underlying hardware supports all the features
+# required to run the Intel AVX-512 implementations of AES-CFB128 algorithms.
+#
+# Returns: non zero if all the required features are detected, 0 otherwise
+#################################################################
+
+.globl   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+.type    ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible,\@abi-omnipotent
+.balign  64
+
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible:
+.cfi_startproc
+    endbranch
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+8(%rip),%ecx
+    xor %eax,%eax
+
+    # Check 3rd 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512BW (bit 30) + AVX512DQ (bit 17) + AVX512F (bit 16)
+
+    and \$0x40030000,%ecx                 # mask is 1<<30|1<<17|1<<16
+    cmp \$0x40030000,%ecx
+    jne .Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+12(%rip),%ecx
+
+    # Check 4th 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512VAES (bit 9)
+
+    and \$0x200,%ecx                      # mask is 1<<9
+    cmp \$0x200,%ecx
+    cmove %ecx,%eax
+
+.Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done:
+    ret
+.cfi_endproc
+.size   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible, .-ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+___
+
+#################################################################
+#
+# AES subroutines for:
+# - preloading the AES key schedule into AVX registers
+# - single-block AES encryption used by CFB encryption and decryption
+# - multiple-block AES encryption used by CFB decryption
+#
+# The CFB mode only uses block cipher encryption.
+#
+# The AES encryption step is described in Section 5.1 Cipher() of
+# FIPS 197 https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197-upd1.pdf
+# and implemented with Intel(R) AES-NI and VAES instructions:
+#
+# - AESKEYGENASSIST for key expansion, elsewhere in aesni_set_encrypt_key()
+# - VPXORD for AES pre-whitening
+# - VAESENC for performing one AES encryption round
+# - VAESENCLAST for performing the last AES encryption round
+#
+# For more information please consult:
+# - the Intel(R) 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual,
+# Chapter 21: Cryptography & Finite Field Arithmetic Instructions
+# https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel64-and-ia32-architectures-optimization.html
+# - the Intel(R) Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) New Instructions Set Whitepaper
+# https://www.intel.com/content/dam/doc/white-paper/advanced-encryption-standard-new-instructions-set-paper.pdf
+#
+#################################################################
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_1x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vmovdqu8   0($key_original),%xmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vmovdqu8  16($key_original),%xmm18  #           1
+    vmovdqu8  32($key_original),%xmm19  #           2
+    vmovdqu8  48($key_original),%xmm20  #           3
+    vmovdqu8  64($key_original),%xmm21  #           4
+    vmovdqu8  80($key_original),%xmm22  #           5
+    vmovdqu8  96($key_original),%xmm23  #           6
+    vmovdqu8 112($key_original),%xmm24  #           7
+    vmovdqu8 128($key_original),%xmm25  #           8
+    vmovdqu8 144($key_original),%xmm26  #           9
+    vmovdqu8 160($key_original),%xmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vmovdqu8 176($key_original),%xmm28  #          11
+    vmovdqu8 192($key_original),%xmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vmovdqu8 208($key_original),%xmm30  #          13
+    vmovdqu8 224($key_original),%xmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds      # load AES rounds
+                                        # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_4x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vbroadcasti32x4   0($key_original),%zmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vbroadcasti32x4  16($key_original),%zmm18  #           1
+    vbroadcasti32x4  32($key_original),%zmm19  #           2
+    vbroadcasti32x4  48($key_original),%zmm20  #           3
+    vbroadcasti32x4  64($key_original),%zmm21  #           4
+    vbroadcasti32x4  80($key_original),%zmm22  #           5
+    vbroadcasti32x4  96($key_original),%zmm23  #           6
+    vbroadcasti32x4 112($key_original),%zmm24  #           7
+    vbroadcasti32x4 128($key_original),%zmm25  #           8
+    vbroadcasti32x4 144($key_original),%zmm26  #           9
+    vbroadcasti32x4 160($key_original),%zmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vbroadcasti32x4 176($key_original),%zmm28  #          11
+    vbroadcasti32x4 192($key_original),%zmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vbroadcasti32x4 208($key_original),%zmm30  #          13
+    vbroadcasti32x4 224($key_original),%zmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds             # load AES rounds
+                                               # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+# Performs AES encryption of 1 128-bit block
+# Expects iv in $temp, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in xmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_1x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %xmm17,$temp,$temp     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %xmm18,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm19,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm20,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm21,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm22,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm23,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm24,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm25,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm26,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm27,$temp,$temp # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm27,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm28,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm29,$temp,$temp # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm29,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm30,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenclast %xmm31,$temp,$temp # last AES-256 encryption round
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_end:
+___
+}
+
+
+# Performs parallel AES encryption of 4 128-bit blocks
+# Expects iv in $temp_4x, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in zmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_4x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %zmm17,$temp_4x,$temp_4x     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm30,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenclast %zmm31,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-256 encryption round
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_end:
+___
+}
+
+
+# Performs parallel AES encryption of 16 128-bit blocks
+# Expects input in $temp_*x, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in zmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_16x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_4x, $temp_4x       # parallel AES pre-whitening
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_16x,$temp_16x

+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256

+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end

+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:

+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_16x,$temp_16x

+    vaesenc %zmm30,$temp_8x, $temp_8x

+    vaesenclast %zmm31,$temp_8x, $temp_8x

+    vaesenclast %zmm31,$temp_16x,$temp_16x

+#################################################################
+# Signature:
+#
+# void ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_enc(
+#     const unsigned char *in,
+#     unsigned char *out,
+#     size_t len,
+#     const AES_KEY *ks,
+#     const unsigned char ivec[16],
+#     /*in-out*/ ossl_ssize_t *num);
+#
+# Preconditions:
+# - all pointers are valid (not NULL...)
+# - AES key schedule and rounds in `ks` are precomputed
+#
+# Invariants:
+# - `*num` is between 0 and 15 (inclusive)
+#
+#################################################################
+#
+# The implementation follows closely the encryption half of CRYPTO_cfb128_encrypt:
+# - "pre" step: processes the last bytes of a partial block
+# - "mid" step: processes complete blocks
+# - "post" step: processes the first bytes of a partial block
+#
+# To obtain the next ciphertext block `cipher <N>` from
+# the plaintext block `plain <N>`, the previous ciphertext
+# block `cipher <N-1>` is required as input.
+#
+# The dependency on previous encryption outputs (ciphertexts)
+# makes CFB encryption inherently serial.
+#
+#                  +----+                       +----------+
+#                  | iv |       +---------------> cipher 0 |
+#                  +--+-+       |               +----------+
+#                     |         |                     |
+#                     |         |                     |
+#              +------v------+  |              +------v------+
+#              | AES encrypt |  |              | AES encrypt |
+#              |  with  key  |  |              |  with  key  |
+#              +------+------+  |              +------+------+

+
+$output = $#ARGV >= 0 && $ARGV[$#ARGV] =~ m|\.\w+$| ? pop : undef;
+$flavour = $#ARGV >= 0 && $ARGV[0] !~ m|\.| ? shift : undef;
+
+$win64=0; $win64=1 if ($flavour =~ /[nm]asm|mingw64/ || $output =~ /\.asm$/);

+
+$0 =~ m/(.*[\/\\])[^\/\\]+$/; $dir=$1;
+( $xlate="${dir}x86_64-xlate.pl" and -f $xlate ) or
+( $xlate="${dir}../../perlasm/x86_64-xlate.pl" and -f $xlate) or
+die "can't locate x86_64-xlate.pl";
+
+if (`$ENV{CC} -Wa,-v -c -o /dev/null -x assembler /dev/null 2>&1`
+        =~ /GNU assembler version ([2-9]\.[0-9]+)/) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1>=2.30);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && $win64 && ($flavour =~ /nasm/ || $ENV{ASM} =~ /nasm/) &&
+       `nasm -v 2>&1` =~ /NASM version ([2-9]\.[0-9]+)(?:\.([0-9]+))?/) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1==2.13 && $2>=3) + ($1>=2.14);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && $win64 && ($flavour =~ /masm/ || $ENV{ASM} =~ /ml64/) &&
+       `ml64 2>&1` =~ /Version ([0-9]+\.[0-9]+)\./) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1>=14.16);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && `$ENV{CC} -v 2>&1`
+    =~ /(Apple)?\s*((?:clang|LLVM) version|.*based on LLVM) ([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)?/) {
+    my $ver = $3 + $4/100.0 + $5/10000.0; # 3.1.0->3.01, 3.10.1->3.1001
+    if ($1) {
+        # Apple conditions, they use a different version series, see
+        # https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xcode#Xcode_7.0_-_10.x_(since_Free_On-Device_Development)_2
+        # clang 7.0.0 is Apple clang 10.0.1
+        $avx512vaes = ($ver>=10.0001)
+    } else {
+        $avx512vaes = ($ver>=7.0);
+    }
+}
+
+open OUT,"| \"$^X\" \"$xlate\" $flavour \"$output\""
+    or die "can't call $xlate: $!";
+*STDOUT=*OUT;
+
+##################################################################
+
+$code=".text\n";
+
+if ($avx512vaes) {
+
+$code.=<<___;
+.extern  OPENSSL_ia32cap_P
+
+#################################################################
+# Signature:
+#
+# int ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible(void);
+#
+# Detects if the underlying hardware supports all the features
+# required to run the Intel AVX-512 implementations of AES-CFB128 algorithms.
+#
+# Returns: non zero if all the required features are detected, 0 otherwise
+#################################################################
+
+.globl   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+.type    ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible,\@abi-omnipotent
+.balign  64
+
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible:
+.cfi_startproc
+    endbranch
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+8(%rip),%ecx
+    xor %eax,%eax
+
+    # Check 3rd 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512BW (bit 30) + AVX512DQ (bit 17) + AVX512F (bit 16)
+
+    and \$0x40030000,%ecx                 # mask is 1<<30|1<<17|1<<16
+    cmp \$0x40030000,%ecx
+    jne .Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+12(%rip),%ecx
+
+    # Check 4th 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512VAES (bit 9)
+
+    and \$0x200,%ecx                      # mask is 1<<9
+    cmp \$0x200,%ecx
+    cmove %ecx,%eax
+
+.Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done:
+    ret
+.cfi_endproc
+.size   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible, .-ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+___
+
+#################################################################
+#
+# AES subroutines for:
+# - preloading the AES key schedule into AVX registers
+# - single-block AES encryption used by CFB encryption and decryption
+# - multiple-block AES encryption used by CFB decryption
+#
+# The CFB mode only uses block cipher encryption.
+#
+# The AES encryption step is described in Section 5.1 Cipher() of
+# FIPS 197 https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197-upd1.pdf
+# and implemented with Intel(R) AES-NI and VAES instructions:
+#
+# - AESKEYGENASSIST for key expansion, elsewhere in aesni_set_encrypt_key()
+# - VPXORD for AES pre-whitening
+# - VAESENC for performing one AES encryption round
+# - VAESENCLAST for performing the last AES encryption round
+#
+# For more information please consult:
+# - the Intel(R) 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual,
+# Chapter 21: Cryptography & Finite Field Arithmetic Instructions
+# https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel64-and-ia32-architectures-optimization.html
+# - the Intel(R) Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) New Instructions Set Whitepaper
+# https://www.intel.com/content/dam/doc/white-paper/advanced-encryption-standard-new-instructions-set-paper.pdf
+#
+#################################################################
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_1x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vmovdqu8   0($key_original),%xmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vmovdqu8  16($key_original),%xmm18  #           1
+    vmovdqu8  32($key_original),%xmm19  #           2
+    vmovdqu8  48($key_original),%xmm20  #           3
+    vmovdqu8  64($key_original),%xmm21  #           4
+    vmovdqu8  80($key_original),%xmm22  #           5
+    vmovdqu8  96($key_original),%xmm23  #           6
+    vmovdqu8 112($key_original),%xmm24  #           7
+    vmovdqu8 128($key_original),%xmm25  #           8
+    vmovdqu8 144($key_original),%xmm26  #           9
+    vmovdqu8 160($key_original),%xmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vmovdqu8 176($key_original),%xmm28  #          11
+    vmovdqu8 192($key_original),%xmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vmovdqu8 208($key_original),%xmm30  #          13
+    vmovdqu8 224($key_original),%xmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds      # load AES rounds
+                                        # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_4x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vbroadcasti32x4   0($key_original),%zmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vbroadcasti32x4  16($key_original),%zmm18  #           1
+    vbroadcasti32x4  32($key_original),%zmm19  #           2
+    vbroadcasti32x4  48($key_original),%zmm20  #           3
+    vbroadcasti32x4  64($key_original),%zmm21  #           4
+    vbroadcasti32x4  80($key_original),%zmm22  #           5
+    vbroadcasti32x4  96($key_original),%zmm23  #           6
+    vbroadcasti32x4 112($key_original),%zmm24  #           7
+    vbroadcasti32x4 128($key_original),%zmm25  #           8
+    vbroadcasti32x4 144($key_original),%zmm26  #           9
+    vbroadcasti32x4 160($key_original),%zmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vbroadcasti32x4 176($key_original),%zmm28  #          11
+    vbroadcasti32x4 192($key_original),%zmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vbroadcasti32x4 208($key_original),%zmm30  #          13
+    vbroadcasti32x4 224($key_original),%zmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds             # load AES rounds
+                                               # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+# Performs AES encryption of 1 128-bit block
+# Expects iv in $temp, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in xmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_1x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %xmm17,$temp,$temp     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %xmm18,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm19,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm20,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm21,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm22,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm23,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm24,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm25,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm26,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm27,$temp,$temp # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm27,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm28,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm29,$temp,$temp # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm29,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm30,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenclast %xmm31,$temp,$temp # last AES-256 encryption round
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_end:
+___
+}
+
+
+# Performs parallel AES encryption of 4 128-bit blocks
+# Expects iv in $temp_4x, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in zmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_4x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %zmm17,$temp_4x,$temp_4x     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm30,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenclast %zmm31,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-256 encryption round

+    valignq \$6,$temp_4x,$cipher_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    lea 64($inp),$inp                           # $inp points to next ciphertext
+___
+
+    &vaes_encrypt_block_4x(".Laes_cfb128_dec_mid_4x");
+
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord $cipher_4x,$temp_4x,$temp_4x         # CipherFeedBack XOR of 4 blocks
+    cmp \$0x40,$len
+    vmovdqu32 $temp_4x,($out)                   # write 4 plaintext blocks
+    vmovdqu8 $cipher_4x,$temp_4x
+    lea 64($out),$out                           # $out points to the next output block
+
+    jae .Loop_aes_cfb128_dec_mid_4x
+
+    vextracti64x2 \$3,$temp_4x,$temp            # latest ciphertext block is next decryption iv
+                                                # move ciphertext3 to position 0 in preparation for next step
+
+    xor %eax,%eax                               # reset $num when processing full blocks
+
+    vmovdqu $temp,($ivp)                        # latest plaintext block is next decryption iv
+
+.Laes_cfb128_dec_check_1x:
+    cmp \$0x10,$len                             # are there full ciphertext blocks left (128 bits) ?
+    jb .Laes_cfb128_dec_post
+
+###########################################################
+# decrypt the rest of full 128-bit blocks in series
+###########################################################
+
+# expects $temp to contain iv
+
+.balign 32
+.Loop_aes_cfb128_dec_mid_1x:
+    sub \$0x10,$len
+
+    vmovdqu ($inp),$cipher            # load ciphertext block
+    lea 16($inp),$inp                 # $inp points to next ciphertext
+___
+
+    &vaes_encrypt_block_1x(".Loop_aes_cfb128_dec_mid_1x_inner");
+
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxor $cipher,$temp,$temp         # CipherFeedBack XOR
+    cmp \$0x10,$len
+    vmovdqu $temp,($out)              # write plaintext
+    vmovdqu8 $cipher,$temp
+    lea 16($out),$out                 # $out points to the next output block
+    jae .Loop_aes_cfb128_dec_mid_1x
+
+    xor %eax,%eax                     # reset $num when processing full blocks
+
+    vmovdqu $temp,($ivp)              # latest plaintext block is next decryption input
+
+.Laes_cfb128_dec_post:
+
+###########################################################
+# last partial block post-processing
+###########################################################
+
+    test $len,$len                     # check if the last block is partial
+    jz .Laes_cfb128_dec_zero_all
+___
+
+    &vaes_encrypt_block_1x(".Loop_aes_cfb128_dec_post");
+
+$code.=<<___;
+
+    mov $len,%rax                      # num=$len
+    mov \$1,%r11                       # build a mask with the least significant $len bits set
+    mov %dl,%cl                        # $len is left shift counter less than 16
+    shlq %cl,%r11
+    dec %r11                           # mask is 2^$len-1
+    kmovq %r11,%k1
+
+    vmovdqu8 ($inp),%xmm1{%k1}{z}      # read $len input bytes, zero the rest to not impact XOR
+    vpxor $temp,%xmm1,%xmm0            # CipherFeedBack XOR
+    vmovdqu8 %xmm0,($out){%k1}         # write $len output bytes
+    vpblendmb %xmm1,$temp,${temp}{%k1} # blend $len input bytes into iv
+
+    vmovdqu8 $temp,($ivp)              # write chained/streaming iv
+
+    # clear registers
+
+.Laes_cfb128_dec_zero_all:
+    vpxord %xmm17,%xmm17,%xmm17        # clear the AES key schedule
+    vpxord %xmm18,%xmm18,%xmm18        # zero the upper lanes of zmm registers
+    vpxord %xmm19,%xmm19,%xmm19
+    vpxord %xmm20,%xmm20,%xmm20
+    vpxord %xmm21,%xmm21,%xmm21
+    vpxord %xmm22,%xmm22,%xmm22
+    vpxord %xmm23,%xmm23,%xmm23
+    vpxord %xmm24,%xmm24,%xmm24
+    vpxord %xmm25,%xmm25,%xmm25
+    vpxord %xmm26,%xmm26,%xmm26
+    vpxord %xmm27,%xmm27,%xmm27
+    vpxord %xmm28,%xmm28,%xmm28
+    vpxord %xmm29,%xmm29,%xmm29
+    vpxord %xmm30,%xmm30,%xmm30
+    vpxord %xmm31,%xmm31,%xmm31
+
+    vpxord %xmm3,%xmm3,%xmm3           # clear registers used during AES encryption
+    vpxord %xmm4,%xmm4,%xmm4
+    vpxord %xmm5,%xmm5,%xmm5
+    vpxord %xmm6,%xmm6,%xmm6
+    vpxord %xmm16,%xmm16,%xmm16
+
+.Laes_cfb128_dec_zero_pre:
+
+    vpxord %xmm0,%xmm0,%xmm0           # clear the rest of the registers
+    vpxord %xmm1,%xmm1,%xmm1
+    vpxord %xmm2,%xmm2,%xmm2
+
+    vzeroupper
+___
+
+$code.=<<___ if($win64);
+    vmovdqu (%rsp),%xmm6               # xmm6 needs to be maintained for Windows
+    add \$16,%rsp
+.cfi_adjust_cfa_offset -16
+___
+
+$code.=<<___;
+    mov %rax,($nump)                   # num is in/out, update for future/chained calls
+
+.Laes_cfb128_vaes_dec_done:
+    ret
+.cfi_endproc
+.size ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_dec,.-ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_dec
+___
+
+} else {
+
+$code .= <<___;
+.globl     ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_enc
+.globl     ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_dec
+
+# Mock implementations of AES-CFB128 encryption/decryption
+# that always fail. Should not be executed under normal circumstances.
+
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_enc:
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_dec:
+    .byte 0x0f,0x0b                # Undefined Instruction in the Intel architecture
+                                   # Raises the Invalid Opcode exception
+    ret
+
+#################################################################
+# Signature:
+#
+# int ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible(void);
+#
+# Always returns 0 (not eligible), meaning that tooling does not support
+# the Intel AVX-512 extensions. Signals higher level code to fallback
+# to an alternative implementation.
+#################################################################
+
+.globl     ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+.type      ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible,\@abi-omnipotent
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible:
+    xor %eax,%eax
+    ret
+.size ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible, .-ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+___
+}
+
+print $code;
+
+close STDOUT or die "error closing STDOUT: $!";

+++ b/crypto/aes/asm/aes-cfb-avx512.pl
@@ -0,0 +1,1033 @@
+#! /usr/bin/env perl
+# Copyright 2025 The OpenSSL Project Authors. All Rights Reserved.
+# Copyright (c) 2025, Intel Corporation. All Rights Reserved.
+#
+# Licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (the "License").  You may not use
+# this file except in compliance with the License.  You can obtain a copy
+# in the file LICENSE in the source distribution or at
+# https://www.openssl.org/source/license.html
+#
+# Implements AES-CFB128 encryption and decryption with Intel(R) VAES
+
+$output = $#ARGV >= 0 && $ARGV[$#ARGV] =~ m|\.\w+$| ? pop : undef;
+$flavour = $#ARGV >= 0 && $ARGV[0] !~ m|\.| ? shift : undef;
+
+$win64=0; $win64=1 if ($flavour =~ /[nm]asm|mingw64/ || $output =~ /\.asm$/);
+
+$avx512vaes=0; # will be non-zero if tooling supports Intel AVX-512 and VAES
+
+$0 =~ m/(.*[\/\\])[^\/\\]+$/; $dir=$1;
+( $xlate="${dir}x86_64-xlate.pl" and -f $xlate ) or
+( $xlate="${dir}../../perlasm/x86_64-xlate.pl" and -f $xlate) or
+die "can't locate x86_64-xlate.pl";
+
+if (`$ENV{CC} -Wa,-v -c -o /dev/null -x assembler /dev/null 2>&1`
+        =~ /GNU assembler version ([2-9]\.[0-9]+)/) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1>=2.30);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && $win64 && ($flavour =~ /nasm/ || $ENV{ASM} =~ /nasm/) &&
+       `nasm -v 2>&1` =~ /NASM version ([2-9]\.[0-9]+)(?:\.([0-9]+))?/) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1==2.13 && $2>=3) + ($1>=2.14);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && $win64 && ($flavour =~ /masm/ || $ENV{ASM} =~ /ml64/) &&
+       `ml64 2>&1` =~ /Version ([0-9]+\.[0-9]+)\./) {
+    $avx512vaes = ($1>=14.16);
+}
+
+if (!$avx512vaes && `$ENV{CC} -v 2>&1`
+    =~ /(Apple)?\s*((?:clang|LLVM) version|.*based on LLVM) ([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)?/) {
+    my $ver = $3 + $4/100.0 + $5/10000.0; # 3.1.0->3.01, 3.10.1->3.1001
+    if ($1) {
+        # Apple conditions, they use a different version series, see
+        # https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xcode#Xcode_7.0_-_10.x_(since_Free_On-Device_Development)_2
+        # clang 7.0.0 is Apple clang 10.0.1
+        $avx512vaes = ($ver>=10.0001)
+    } else {
+        $avx512vaes = ($ver>=7.0);
+    }
+}
+
+open OUT,"| \"$^X\" \"$xlate\" $flavour \"$output\""
+    or die "can't call $xlate: $!";
+*STDOUT=*OUT;
+
+##################################################################
+
+$code=".text\n";
+
+if ($avx512vaes) {
+
+$code.=<<___;
+.extern  OPENSSL_ia32cap_P
+
+#################################################################
+# Signature:
+#
+# int ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible(void);
+#
+# Detects if the underlying hardware supports all the features
+# required to run the Intel AVX-512 implementations of AES-CFB128 algorithms.
+#
+# Returns: non zero if all the required features are detected, 0 otherwise
+#################################################################
+
+.globl   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+.type    ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible,\@abi-omnipotent
+.balign  64
+
+ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible:
+.cfi_startproc
+    endbranch
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+8(%rip),%ecx
+    xor %eax,%eax
+
+    # Check 3rd 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512BW (bit 30) + AVX512DQ (bit 17) + AVX512F (bit 16)
+
+    and \$0x40030000,%ecx                 # mask is 1<<30|1<<17|1<<16
+    cmp \$0x40030000,%ecx
+    jne .Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done
+
+    mov OPENSSL_ia32cap_P+12(%rip),%ecx
+
+    # Check 4th 32-bit word of OPENSSL_ia32cap_P for the feature bit(s):
+    # AVX512VAES (bit 9)
+
+    and \$0x200,%ecx                      # mask is 1<<9
+    cmp \$0x200,%ecx
+    cmove %ecx,%eax
+
+.Laes_cfb128_vaes_eligible_done:
+    ret
+.cfi_endproc
+.size   ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible, .-ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_eligible
+___
+
+#################################################################
+#
+# AES subroutines for:
+# - preloading the AES key schedule into AVX registers
+# - single-block AES encryption used by CFB encryption and decryption
+# - multiple-block AES encryption used by CFB decryption
+#
+# The CFB mode only uses block cipher encryption.
+#
+# The AES encryption step is described in Section 5.1 Cipher() of
+# FIPS 197 https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197-upd1.pdf
+# and implemented with Intel(R) AES-NI and VAES instructions:
+#
+# - AESKEYGENASSIST for key expansion, elsewhere in aesni_set_encrypt_key()
+# - VPXORD for AES pre-whitening
+# - VAESENC for performing one AES encryption round
+# - VAESENCLAST for performing the last AES encryption round
+#
+# For more information please consult:
+# - the Intel(R) 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual,
+# Chapter 21: Cryptography & Finite Field Arithmetic Instructions
+# https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel64-and-ia32-architectures-optimization.html
+# - the Intel(R) Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) New Instructions Set Whitepaper
+# https://www.intel.com/content/dam/doc/white-paper/advanced-encryption-standard-new-instructions-set-paper.pdf
+#
+#################################################################
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_1x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vmovdqu8   0($key_original),%xmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vmovdqu8  16($key_original),%xmm18  #           1
+    vmovdqu8  32($key_original),%xmm19  #           2
+    vmovdqu8  48($key_original),%xmm20  #           3
+    vmovdqu8  64($key_original),%xmm21  #           4
+    vmovdqu8  80($key_original),%xmm22  #           5
+    vmovdqu8  96($key_original),%xmm23  #           6
+    vmovdqu8 112($key_original),%xmm24  #           7
+    vmovdqu8 128($key_original),%xmm25  #           8
+    vmovdqu8 144($key_original),%xmm26  #           9
+    vmovdqu8 160($key_original),%xmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vmovdqu8 176($key_original),%xmm28  #          11
+    vmovdqu8 192($key_original),%xmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vmovdqu8 208($key_original),%xmm30  #          13
+    vmovdqu8 224($key_original),%xmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds      # load AES rounds
+                                        # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+
+# expects the key schedule address in $key_original
+sub load_aes_key_schedule_4x() {
+$code.=<<___;
+    vbroadcasti32x4   0($key_original),%zmm17  # schedule  0 whitening
+    vbroadcasti32x4  16($key_original),%zmm18  #           1
+    vbroadcasti32x4  32($key_original),%zmm19  #           2
+    vbroadcasti32x4  48($key_original),%zmm20  #           3
+    vbroadcasti32x4  64($key_original),%zmm21  #           4
+    vbroadcasti32x4  80($key_original),%zmm22  #           5
+    vbroadcasti32x4  96($key_original),%zmm23  #           6
+    vbroadcasti32x4 112($key_original),%zmm24  #           7
+    vbroadcasti32x4 128($key_original),%zmm25  #           8
+    vbroadcasti32x4 144($key_original),%zmm26  #           9
+    vbroadcasti32x4 160($key_original),%zmm27  #          10 last for AES-128
+    vbroadcasti32x4 176($key_original),%zmm28  #          11
+    vbroadcasti32x4 192($key_original),%zmm29  #          12 last for AES-192
+    vbroadcasti32x4 208($key_original),%zmm30  #          13
+    vbroadcasti32x4 224($key_original),%zmm31  #          14 last for AES-256
+
+    mov 240($key_original),$rounds             # load AES rounds
+                                               # 240 is the byte-offset of the rounds field in AES_KEY
+___
+}
+
+# Performs AES encryption of 1 128-bit block
+# Expects iv in $temp, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in xmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_1x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %xmm17,$temp,$temp     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %xmm18,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm19,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm20,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm21,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm22,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm23,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm24,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm25,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm26,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm27,$temp,$temp # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm27,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm28,$temp,$temp
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %xmm29,$temp,$temp # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %xmm29,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenc %xmm30,$temp,$temp
+    vaesenclast %xmm31,$temp,$temp # last AES-256 encryption round
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_end:
+___
+}
+
+
+# Performs parallel AES encryption of 4 128-bit blocks
+# Expects iv in $temp_4x, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in zmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_4x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord  %zmm17,$temp_4x,$temp_4x     # AES pre-whitening
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm26,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x09,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_192_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-128 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_192_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm27,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm28,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+
+    cmp \$0x0B,$rounds
+    ja ${label_prefix}_256
+
+    vaesenclast %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-192 encryption round
+    jmp ${label_prefix}_end
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_256:
+
+    vaesenc %zmm29,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm30,$temp_4x,$temp_4x
+    vaesenclast %zmm31,$temp_4x,$temp_4x # last AES-256 encryption round
+
+.balign 32
+${label_prefix}_end:
+___
+}
+
+
+# Performs parallel AES encryption of 16 128-bit blocks
+# Expects input in $temp_*x, non-final AES rounds in $rounds and key schedule in zmm17..31
+sub vaes_encrypt_block_16x() {
+    my ($label_prefix)=@_;
+$code.=<<___;
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_4x, $temp_4x       # parallel AES pre-whitening
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vpxord %zmm17,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm18,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm19,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm20,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm21,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm22,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm23,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm24,$temp_16x,$temp_16x
+
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_4x, $temp_4x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_8x, $temp_8x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_12x,$temp_12x
+    vaesenc %zmm25,$temp_16x,$temp_16x

findings.message: The partial-block pre-processing code in ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_enc and ossl_aes_cfb128_vaes_dec unconditionally loads 16 bytes from the input buffer using unmasked vmovdqu8 instructions, even when fewer bytes are valid. When processing partial blocks (where $left contains 1-15 valid bytes), the vmovdqu8 (%r11),%xmm0 and vmovdqu8 ($inp),%xmm1 instructions always load a full 16-byte vector. This can read 1-15 bytes beyond the valid buffer boundary. If the input buffer ends at a memory page boundary and the following page is unmapped, this triggers a crash leading to denial of service. Notably, the post-processing code in the same file correctly uses masked loads with {%k1}{z} to avoid this issue, but this pattern was not consistently applied in the pre-processing section.
findings.suggestion: Use masked vmovdqu8 loads with the {%k1}{z} suffix to only load valid bytes. The mask register k1 already contains the correct bitmask for the valid bytes (set earlier via kmovq $mask,%k1). Change 'vmovdqu8 (%r11),%xmm0' to 'vmovdqu8 (%r11),%xmm0{%k1}{z}' and 'vmovdqu8 ($inp),%xmm1' to 'vmovdqu8 ($inp),%xmm1{%k1}{z}'.

ground_truth.root_cause: Inconsistent use of masked vs unmasked AVX-512 load instructions. agent_reasoning: The vulnerability was a NULL pointer dereference in check_delta_base() in crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c. The original code called ASN1_INTEGER_cmp(delta->crl_number, base->crl_number) without first verifying that delta->crl_number was non-NULL. A malformed delta CRL could have the Delta CRL Indicator extension (setting base_crl_number) but lack the CRL Number extension (leaving crl_number as NULL), causing a crash when ASN1_INTEGER_cmp dereferenced it. The fix adds an explicit NULL guard — `if (delta->crl_number == NULL) return 0;` — immediately before the comparison, so that such malformed CRLs are cleanly rejected rather than causing a crash. The on-disk code avoids the vulnerability by always checking delta->crl_number for NULL before use.

intro_commit_message: Initial support for delta CRLs. If "use deltas" flag is set attempt to find a delta CRL in addition to a full CRL. Check and search delta in addition to the base.
pr_description:
## Summary

When processing delta CRLs with `X509_V_FLAG_USE_DELTAS` enabled, the `check_delta_base()` function in `crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c` validates several conditions before comparing CRL numbers. However, it was missing a NULL check for `delta->crl_number` before passing it to `ASN1_INTEGER_cmp()`.

A well-formed delta CRL must contain both a Delta CRL Indicator extension (which populates `base_crl_number`) and a CRL Number extension (which populates `crl_number`). The existing code correctly checked that `delta->base_crl_number` and `base->crl_number` are non-NULL, but assumed `delta->crl_number` would always be present if `base_crl_number` was present. This assumption does not hold for malformed or attacker-crafted CRL files.

## Changes

- Added an explicit NULL check for `delta->crl_number` in `check_delta_base()` before calling `ASN1_INTEGER_cmp()`. If the delta CRL is missing the CRL Number extension, the function now returns 0 (reject) instead of dereferencing a NULL pointer.
- Simplified the final comparison to a direct `return` expression, removing the now-redundant if/else structure.

## Impact

Without this check, an attacker who can supply a crafted delta CRL file (one containing a Delta CRL Indicator extension but no CRL Number extension) can trigger a NULL pointer dereference, causing a crash in any application that enables delta CRL verification via `X509_V_FLAG_USE_DELTAS`.
pr_title: Fix NULL dereference in check_delta_base() when delta CRL lacks CRL Number extension

findings.message: The check_delta_base() function validates that delta->base_crl_number and base->crl_number are not NULL before use, but fails to validate delta->crl_number before passing it to ASN1_INTEGER_cmp(). When a malformed delta CRL contains the Delta CRL Indicator extension (base_crl_number) but lacks the required CRL Number extension (crl_number), the delta->crl_number field will be NULL. The subsequent call to ASN1_INTEGER_cmp(delta->crl_number, base->crl_number) dereferences this NULL pointer, causing a crash. This vulnerability is exploitable when X509_V_FLAG_USE_DELTAS is enabled and an attacker can supply a crafted CRL file.

related_locations.description: NULL check for base->crl_number exists, but missing check for delta->crl_number

findings.suggestion: Add a NULL check for delta->crl_number before calling ASN1_INTEGER_cmp(). Return 0 if delta->crl_number is NULL, as a delta CRL without a CRL Number extension is malformed and should be rejected.

ground_truth.root_cause: The check_delta_base() function was implemented with incomplete input validation. While it correctly checks that delta->base_crl_number is not NULL (to verify the CRL is actually a delta CRL) and that base->crl_number is not NULL (to ensure the base CRL has a number to compare against), it assumes delta->crl_number will always be present when base_crl_number is present. This assumption is incorrect - a malformed CRL can have one extension without the other.

pr_title: Initial support for delta CRLs. If "use deltas" flag is set attempt to find a delta CRL in addition to a full CRL. Check and search delta in addition to the base.

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability would have been a NULL pointer dereference in `dh_cms_set_shared_info()` (in `crypto/dh/dh_ameth.c`) and `ecdh_cms_set_shared_info()` (in `crypto/ec/ec_ameth.c`). Both functions directly accessed `alg->algorithm` and `alg->parameter->type` without first checking if `alg->parameter` was NULL. Since the `parameters` field of `AlgorithmIdentifier` is optional in ASN.1 (RFC 5652), a crafted CMS message that omits the parameter field would result in `alg->parameter` being NULL, causing a SIGSEGV when the code tries to read `alg->parameter->type`. The fix uses `X509_ALGOR_get0()` to extract the OID and parameter type/value atomically into local variables (`aoid`, `atype`, `aval`), then checks `atype != V_ASN1_SEQUENCE` before accessing the parameter value. This ensures a NULL parameter is caught safely as a type mismatch rather than causing a crash.

fix_commit_message:
Fix NULL deref in [ec]dh_cms_set_shared_info

Multiple independent reports indicated a SIGSEGV was possible in CMS
processing when a crafted CMS EnvelopedData message using A Key
Agreement Recipient Info field.  If the
KeyEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier omits the optional parameter field, the
referenced functions above will attempt to dereference the
alg->parameter data prior to checking if the parameter field is NULL.

Confirmed to resolve the issues using the reproducers provided in the
security reports.

Co-authored-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.foundation>

Fixes CVE-2026-28389

intro_commit_message: CMS RFC2631 X9.42 DH enveloped data support.
pr_description:
This PR adds CMS KeyAgreeRecipientInfo support for DH (RFC2631 X9.42) and ECDH key agreement, allowing OpenSSL to encrypt and decrypt CMS EnvelopedData messages using key agreement recipient info.

The implementation adds `dh_cms_set_peerkey`, `dh_cms_set_shared_info`, `dh_cms_decrypt`, and `dh_cms_encrypt` to `crypto/dh/dh_ameth.c`, and corresponding `ecdh_cms_set_peerkey`, `ecdh_cms_set_shared_info`, `ecdh_cms_decrypt`, and `ecdh_cms_encrypt` to `crypto/ec/ec_ameth.c`.

For both DH and ECDH, the shared info functions use `X509_ALGOR_get0()` to safely extract the algorithm OID and parameters from the `X509_ALGOR` structure before accessing them. This approach correctly handles the case where the optional `parameters` field of the `KeyEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier` is absent — checking the parameter type variable (`atype`) against `V_ASN1_SEQUENCE` before any attempt to read parameter data, and using `ASN1_STRING_data`/`ASN1_STRING_length` accessors rather than direct struct member access.

The `pkey_ctrl` handlers for both DH and ECDH are wired up to route `ASN1_PKEY_CTRL_CMS_ENVELOPE` and `ASN1_PKEY_CTRL_CMS_RI_TYPE` operations through the new CMS functions.
pr_title: CMS RFC2631 X9.42 DH and ECDH enveloped data support with safe parameter handling

findings.message: The function dh_cms_set_shared_info() directly dereferences alg->parameter without first checking if it is NULL. When processing a CMS EnvelopedData message with KeyAgreeRecipientInfo, the optional 'parameters' field of KeyEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier may be absent (NULL). Accessing alg->parameter->type when alg->parameter is NULL causes a NULL pointer dereference, leading to a crash (SIGSEGV). This vulnerability can be triggered by an attacker sending a crafted CMS message to any application that calls CMS_decrypt() on untrusted input, such as S/MIME processing or CMS-based protocols, resulting in Denial of Service before any authentication or cryptographic operations occur.
findings.suggestion: Use X509_ALGOR_get0() to safely extract the algorithm parameters before accessing them. This function returns the parameter type and value without dereferencing a potentially NULL pointer. Check the returned ptype value before accessing the parameter data.
findings.title: NULL Pointer Dereference in CMS KeyAgreeRecipientInfo Parameter Handling

pr_description:
Add overflow guards to `buf2hexstr_sep` and `openssl_buf2hexstr_sep` before computing the required output buffer size.

Previously, the buffer size was calculated as `buflen * 3` (with separator) or `1 + buflen * 2` (without separator) without any range check. On 32-bit platforms where `size_t` is 32 bits, sufficiently large values of `buflen` (~1.4 GB+) cause the multiplication to wrap around to a small value. The undersized buffer is then allocated and the subsequent conversion loop writes far beyond the end of it, causing a heap buffer overflow.

This PR introduces explicit overflow checks before the size calculation in both functions:

- In `buf2hexstr_sep`: check `buflen > SIZE_MAX / 3` (or `(SIZE_MAX - 1) / 2` without separator) and return an error immediately.
- In `openssl_buf2hexstr_sep`: the same bounds check using `(size_t)buflen` casts on the `long` parameter, and update the `tmp_n` assignment to use explicit `(size_t)` casts to avoid implicit narrowing.

Both paths raise `CRYPTO_R_TOO_MANY_BYTES` so callers receive a clear diagnostic.

Callers that pass an attacker-controlled buffer length — for example when printing X.509 extension values such as Subject Key Identifier or Authority Key Identifier — are now protected against heap corruption on platforms with small `size_t`.
pr_title: Avoid integer overflow in buf2hexstr conversion when buflen is very large

findings.message: The function openssl_buf2hexstr_sep (later renamed ossl_buf2hexstr_sep) calculates the output buffer size for hexadecimal string conversion using the expression `buflen * 3` or `1 + buflen * 2`. On 32-bit platforms, when buflen exceeds approximately SIZE_MAX/3 (around 1.4GB), this multiplication overflows, wrapping around to a small value. The undersized buffer is then allocated with OPENSSL_malloc(), and the subsequent buf2hexstr_sep() call writes far beyond the allocated memory, causing a heap buffer overflow. An attacker can trigger this by providing a crafted X.509 certificate with an excessively large OCTET STRING value in extensions like Subject Key Identifier (SKID) or Authority Key Identifier (AKID) that are converted to hex for printing or logging.
findings.suggestion: Add overflow checks before the multiplication to ensure the result does not exceed SIZE_MAX. Check if buflen > SIZE_MAX / 3 (when separator is present) or buflen > (SIZE_MAX - 1) / 2 (when no separator) before computing the buffer size. Also add a check for negative buflen values since the parameter type is long.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 5097ec4dae23 on top of intro 96075a6a4061 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The OpenSSL QUIC server's port_default_packet_handler() (ssl/quic/quic_port.c) mishandles the lifetime tracking of the OSSL_QRX (QUIC record-layer receive) object used to validate an Initial packet's AEAD/integrity when address validation is disabled. The function stores the validated qrx pointer into a secondary variable qrx_src (and clears qrx) in two separate code paths: (1) unconditionally when validate_addr == 0 right after packet validation succeeds, and (2) again when a supplied token fails validation and validate_addr == 0. The second occurrence blindly reassigns qrx_src from qrx without checking that qrx is non-NULL, so it overwrites the already-saved qrx_src with NULL. The function then dereferences qrx_src (via ossl_qrx_read_pkt()/ossl_qrx_update_pn_space()) believing it holds the salvaged QRX, resulting in a NULL pointer dereference and process crash. Root cause: Missing NULL-check before reassigning the qrx_src 'forget qrx' bookkeeping variable in a second code path that can execute after the first 'forget qrx' path already cleared qrx to NULL, causing the previously valid qrx_src to be silently overwritten with NULL and later dereferenced.
commit_message:
Fix AEAD validation of initial packets in port

The interoperability tests disable client ip address
validation done by RETRY packet. All tests done in CI
take code path which sends a retry packet.

The first initial packet sent by client uses a different
initial encryption level keys to protect packet integrity.
The keys are derived from DCID chosen by client.

When server accepts connection on behalf of initial packet,
the 'DCID' gets changed which means the initial level encryption keys
are changing too. So when server skips sending a retry packet,
it must forget the qrx which was used to validate initial
packet sent by client.

Forgetting qrx is not straightforward, we must salvage the
unencrypted packets left there after they were validated.
Those unencrypted packets must be injected to newly created channel.

Reviewed-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26808)

findings.message: In port_default_packet_handler(), when address validation is disabled (port->validate_addr == 0), the function performs 'qrx_src = qrx; qrx = NULL;' immediately after ossl_qrx_validate_initial_packet() succeeds, in order to remember the just-validated QRX so its buffered packets can later be salvaged into the new channel. Later in the same function, if the client also supplied a token (hdr.token != NULL) and port_validate_token() fails, the code re-enters the same-looking assignment 'qrx_src = qrx; qrx = NULL;' inside the (port->validate_addr == 0) fallback branch of the token-validation-failure handling, WITHOUT checking whether qrx is already NULL (which it always is at that point, since it was already nulled out by the first block above). This overwrites the previously saved qrx_src pointer with NULL, discarding the only reference to the validated QRX object. Execution then falls through to port_bind_channel() with qrx == NULL; since qrx is NULL, the 'else' branch is taken which calls 'ossl_qrx_read_pkt(qrx_src, &qrx_pkt)' with qrx_src == NULL, dereferencing a NULL pointer inside ossl_qrx_read_pkt() and crashing the server process. This is remotely triggerable by a single attacker-controlled QUIC Initial packet that carries an invalid/expired token when the listener was created with SSL_LISTENER_FLAG_NO_VALIDATE (address validation disabled).
findings.suggestion: Guard the second 'forget qrx' assignment with a check that qrx is not already NULL before overwriting qrx_src, exactly as later fixed: only perform 'qrx_src = qrx; qrx = NULL;' when qrx != NULL. This prevents clobbering a previously salvaged qrx_src pointer and avoids handing a NULL pointer to ossl_qrx_read_pkt()/ossl_qrx_update_pn_space() downstream.
findings.title: Unconditional reassignment of qrx_src can null out a previously salvaged QRX pointer, causing later NULL dereference

fix_commit.message: Fix NULL dereference in QUIC address validation

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Unconditional reassignment of qrx_src can null out a previously salvaged QRX pointer, causing later NULL dereference

ground_truth.root_cause: Missing NULL-check before reassigning the qrx_src 'forget qrx' bookkeeping variable in a second code path that can execute after the first 'forget qrx' path already cleared qrx to NULL, causing the previously valid qrx_src to be silently overwritten with NULL and later dereferenced.

pr_description:
The interoperability tests disable client ip address
validation done by RETRY packet. All tests done in CI
take code path which sends a retry packet.

The first initial packet sent by client uses a different
initial encryption level keys to protect packet integrity.
The keys are derived from DCID chosen by client.

When server accepts connection on behalf of initial packet,
the 'DCID' gets changed which means the initial level encryption keys
are changing too. So when server skips sending a retry packet,
it must forget the qrx which was used to validate initial
packet sent by client.

Forgetting qrx is not straightforward, we must salvage the
unencrypted packets left there after they were validated.
Those unencrypted packets must be injected to newly created channel.

Reviewed-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26808)
pr_title: Fix AEAD validation of initial packets in port

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added a new EVP_PKEY_CTX control to disable RSA implicit rejection, and separately (and incorrectly) used that control inside CMS's ktri decrypt path, defeating the Bleichenbacher/Marvin-attack mitigation for CMS RSA key-transport recipients. The fix commit removes only the disablement inside cms_env.c (the PKCS7 counterpart was not part of this intro commit, since the intro commit only touched cms_env.c, not pk7_doit.c), leaving the new opt-out control itself intact for other callers, and adds documentation clarifying the implicit-rejection behaviour for CMS_decrypt/PKCS7_decrypt callers. I mirrored that: removed the EVP_PKEY_is_a(pkey, "RSA") / EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str("rsa_pkcs1_implicit_rejection","0") block from crypto/cms/cms_env.c, and applied the corresponding doc/man3/CMS_decrypt.pod and doc/man3/PKCS7_decrypt.pod wording changes from the fix diff, without touching pk7_doit.c since it does not contain the disablement in this snapshot (that code path was introduced by a separate, later commit not reachable from this intro commit).

findings.message:
cms_RecipientInfo_ktri_decrypt() (and its PKCS#7 counterpart pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(), added shortly after in commit 056dade341d) explicitly disables the RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 'implicit rejection' countermeasure by calling EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str(ktri->pctx, "rsa_pkcs1_implicit_rejection", "0") right after the decrypt context is created, whenever the recipient key is RSA. Implicit rejection is the modern constant-behavior mitigation (per draft-irtf-cfrg-rsa-guidance) against Bleichenbacher-style adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks on PKCS#1 v1.5 key transport: instead of returning distinguishable success/failure for valid vs. invalid padding, the RSA decryption operation always 'succeeds' and instead returns a deterministic pseudo-random value derived from the ciphertext and private key when padding is invalid, so an attacker cannot use error codes or decrypted output differences as an oracle.

By turning this protection off for RSA keys used in CMS/PKCS#7 decryption, the code reintroduces the classic multi-RecipientInfo Bleichenbacher oracle: CMS_decrypt()/PKCS7_decrypt() iterate over every KeyTransRecipientInfo (when no recipient certificate is supplied) or substitute a random key when the recipient isn't matched, and now genuinely propagate distinguishable PKCS#1 padding-valid/invalid behavior (real decrypt success vs. hard failure) to callers who can observe error codes or decryption results. An attacker who crafts a CMS/S-MIME message with a probe RecipientInfo can use the victim's decrypting application as a decryption/signing oracle against the victim's RSA private key.

The comment justifying the disablement ('upper layer CMS code incorrectly assumes that a successful RSA decryption means that the key matches ciphertext') reveals the root cause: the CMS/PKCS7 layer's control flow depends on being able to distinguish RSA decryption success from failure, so implicit rejection (which never reports failure) was turned off instead of fixing that layer's logic — trading away a security mitigation for internal implementation convenience.
findings.suggestion: Do not disable the RSA implicit-rejection mitigation. Remove the EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str(..., "rsa_pkcs1_implicit_rejection", "0") calls in cms_RecipientInfo_ktri_decrypt() and pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(), and instead fix the upper-layer CMS/PKCS7 code so it no longer relies on a distinguishable RSA decrypt success/failure signal to select a RecipientInfo or to detect key mismatch (e.g. always require/validate an explicit recipient certificate, and treat all RSA decryptions as always-succeeding with a fixed-length/random fallback key on padding failure, consistent with implicit rejection semantics).
findings.title: Explicit disabling of RSA implicit rejection re-opens Bleichenbacher oracle in CMS/PKCS#7 RSA key-transport decryption

fix_commit.author: Dmitry Belyavskiy
fix_commit.message: Enforce implicit rejection for CMS/PKCS#7 decryption

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Explicit disabling of RSA implicit rejection re-opens Bleichenbacher oracle in CMS/PKCS#7 RSA key-transport decryption

ground_truth.root_cause: commit 5ab3ec1bb1e (and its PKCS7 counterpart 056dade341d) added code to explicitly turn off the RSA 'implicit rejection' Bleichenbacher countermeasure (EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str with "rsa_pkcs1_implicit_rejection"="0") inside cms_RecipientInfo_ktri_decrypt()/pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(), because the surrounding CMS/PKCS7 logic incorrectly relied on being able to distinguish a successful RSA PKCS#1 decryption from a failed one to decide whether a given RecipientInfo matched. This traded away a modern anti-Bleichenbacher mitigation for internal control-flow convenience, restoring a distinguishable success/failure oracle in multi-recipient or certificate-less decryption scenarios.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c2765d53c264 on top of intro 01b048513153 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): OSSL_CMP_get1_rootCaKeyUpdate() processes CMP genp id-it-rootCaKeyUpdate messages that transfer trust from an old root CA key to a new root CA key. Verifying the 'newWithOld' certificate's signature (i.e. that the new root cert is signed by the old root CA private key) is essential to this trust transfer. The verification is implemented via a custom X509_STORE_CTX verify callback, selfsigned_verify_cb(), invoked from verify_ss_cert(). Due to a typo, the callback appended the target certificate itself ('cert') to the verification chain instead of the discovered trusted issuer certificate ('issuer'). This meant the certificate chain built for verification did not actually contain the real old root CA certificate, so X509_verify_cert() could not correctly validate that the new root certificate was signed by the old root key. Combined with self-signed signature checking not being explicitly enabled, the validation was effectively reduced to checking only the issuer name and algorithm OIDs, not the actual cryptographic signature linking old and new root certificates. Root cause: A single-character/variable-name typo in selfsigned_verify_cb() (using 'cert' instead of 'issuer' as the argument to X509_add_cert() when building the verification chain) caused the wrong certificate to be added to the chain used for verifying the newWithOld self-signed root certificate, rendering the cryptographic signature check ineffective.

fix_commit_message:
Use the correct issuer when validating rootCAKeyUpdate

This correctly uses the existing root, and not the same certificate
as the root of the chain to validate.

While we are here, we also turn on self signed certificate signature
checking as this case is actually bringing in trust anchors as
self signed certs, and fix a possible NULL deref.

Fixes CVE-2026-42769

findings.message: The custom X509_STORE_CTX verify callback selfsigned_verify_cb(), used by verify_ss_cert()/verify_ss_cert_trans() when validating the 'newWithOld' self-signed certificate received in a CMP genp id-it-rootCaKeyUpdate message, is supposed to append the trusted 'issuer' certificate (the old root CA cert found via check_issued) to the chain so that X509_verify_cert() can subsequently check the self-signature of the target ('newWithOld') using that issuer's public key. Instead, the code adds 'cert' (which at this point is still bound to the target/self-signed certificate itself, i.e. the same certificate being validated) rather than 'issuer' to the chain. Because the chain now consists of the target certificate followed by itself instead of the target certificate followed by its real issuer (the old root CA), the subsequent verification of the certificate's signature effectively degenerates into verifying the certificate against itself (or otherwise fails to properly bind the new root cert to the old root's key), and the check_issued/verify_cb logic reports 'ok' even though no genuine cryptographic link between the old and new root certificates was established. As a result, an attacker with valid RA-level protection credentials for the CMP exchange can supply a self-signed, attacker-generated 'newWithOld' certificate that the client will accept as a legitimate, cryptographically-verified new root CA trust anchor, escalating from RA-level credentials to root CA-level trust.
findings.suggestion: In selfsigned_verify_cb(), when check_issued() identifies the matching trust-anchor certificate, add that 'issuer' certificate to the chain (not 'cert', which is the target certificate under validation), so that the subsequent verification of the self-signed target certificate's signature is actually performed against the correct old root CA public key. Additionally, ensure X509_V_FLAG_CHECK_SS_SIGNATURE is set on the verification context so self-signed certificate signatures are checked at all, since X509_verify_cert() otherwise skips signature checks for self-signed target certificates by default.
findings.title: Wrong certificate added to chain in selfsigned_verify_cb() bypasses signature verification of rootCaKeyUpdate trust anchor

fix_commit.author: Bob Beck
fix_commit.message: Use the correct issuer when validating rootCAKeyUpdate

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Wrong certificate added to chain in selfsigned_verify_cb() bypasses signature verification of rootCaKeyUpdate trust anchor

ground_truth.root_cause: A single-character/variable-name typo in selfsigned_verify_cb() (using 'cert' instead of 'issuer' as the argument to X509_add_cert() when building the verification chain) caused the wrong certificate to be added to the chain used for verifying the newWithOld self-signed root certificate, rendering the cryptographic signature check ineffective.

pr_title: CMP: add support for genm with rootCaCert and genp with rootCaKeyUpdate

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added validate_email_name() with a length-calculation bug: local_len was computed as len - (at - name) (the trailing length from '@' onward) rather than at - name (the actual local-part length before '@'), and validate_local_part() was invoked with the original full len instead of the corrected local_len. This caused validate_local_part()'s scanning loop to run over bytes beyond the true local part, producing an out-of-bounds read (CVE-2026-42771). I applied the minimal fix: set local_len = at - name, and pass local_len (not len) into validate_local_part(). This mirrors the upstream fix commit's core semantic change to x509_vpm.c. I left validate_hostname_part() untouched because this worktree's implementation of that function is already structured differently from the upstream pre-fix code shown in the reference diff (its part_len increment is unconditional after the if/else rather than inside the else-branch as in the diff's before-state), so the literal hunk does not correspond to on-disk code and forcing it in would constitute an unrelated/incorrect refactor unconnected to the CVE, which only concerns the email local-part length bug.
commit_message:
Let's support multiple names for certificate verification

This adds the functionality to VERIFY_PARAM to separately add multiple
ip's and email addresses for verification purposes.

We then mark the unfortunate SSL_add1_host API which unfortunately
aquired a confusing "maybe add an IP address" behaviour as deprecated.

We replace this with SSL_set1_<dnsname, email, ip, ip_asc> and
SSL_add1_<dnsname, email, ip, ip_asc> to set the things in the SSL
corresponding to the VERIFY_PARAM funcitons.

Fixes: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/28418

Reviewed-by: Viktor Dukhovni <viktor@openssl.org>

+++ b/doc/man3/SSL_CTX_dane_enable.pod
@@ -59,21 +59,21 @@ By default, matching type C<SHA2-256(1)> (see RFC7218 for definitions
 of the DANE TLSA parameter acronyms) is mapped to C<EVP_sha256()>
 with a strength ordinal of C<1> and matching type C<SHA2-512(2)>
 is mapped to C<EVP_sha512()> with a strength ordinal of C<2>.
 
 SSL_dane_enable() must be called before the SSL handshake is initiated with
 L<SSL_connect(3)> if (and only if) you want to enable DANE for that connection.
 (The connection must be associated with a DANE-enabled SSL context).
 The B<basedomain> argument specifies the RFC7671 TLSA base domain,
 which will be the primary peer reference identifier for certificate
 name checks.
-Additional server names can be specified via L<SSL_add1_host(3)>.
+Additional server names can be specified via L<SSL_add1_dnsname(3)>.
 The B<basedomain> is used as the default SNI hint if none has yet been
 specified via L<SSL_set_tlsext_host_name(3)>.
 
 SSL_dane_tlsa_add() may then be called one or more times, to load each of the
 TLSA records that apply to the remote TLS peer.
 (This too must be done prior to the beginning of the SSL handshake).
 The arguments specify the fields of the TLSA record.
 The B<data> field is provided in binary (wire RDATA) form, not the hexadecimal

Fix length miscalculation in validate_email

when validating e-mail for X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_email().

Fixes CVE-2026-42771

intro_commit_message:
Let's support multiple names for certificate verification

This adds the functionality to VERIFY_PARAM to separately add multiple
ip's and email addresses for verification purposes.

We then mark the unfortunate SSL_add1_host API which unfortunately
aquired a confusing "maybe add an IP address" behaviour as deprecated.

We replace this with SSL_set1_<dnsname, email, ip, ip_asc> and
SSL_add1_<dnsname, email, ip, ip_asc> to set the things in the SSL
corresponding to the VERIFY_PARAM funcitons.

Fixes: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/28418

Reviewed-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Viktor Dukhovni <viktor@openssl.org>

findings.message: validate_email_name() computes local_len as 'len - (at - name)' where 'at' points to the '@' character. This is actually the length of the remainder of the string starting at '@' (i.e. domain length + 1), not the length of the local part before '@' (which should be 'at - name'). This wrong value is then (a) used incorrectly to bound-check the 64-octet local-part limit (so the real local part length is never actually checked, allowing local parts far longer than 64 octets to pass), and (b) passed as the 'len' argument together with the full original buffer to validate_local_part(name, len, &local_charset) -- note it actually passes the original 'len' (the whole email length) instead of the corrected local part length, causing validate_local_part to iterate past the end of the local part and, since len can be up to 320 while name only has 'at - name' valid local-part bytes before the caller-supplied length boundary, this can walk beyond the intended field and, depending on how the buffer was allocated/null-terminated by the caller (e.g., during S/MIME From: address parsing), read out of bounds. This is reachable from the public API X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_email()/X509_VERIFY_PARAM_add1_email(), and from S/MIME message validation when a crafted From: address is supplied, potentially resulting in a crash (DoS).
findings.suggestion: Compute local_len as the distance from the start of the string to the '@' character (at - name), not as len minus that distance. Then pass this corrected local_len (not the full len) to validate_local_part() so it only scans the actual local part bytes.
findings.title: Wrong length used for local-part validation in validate_email_name() causes OOB read

agent_reasoning: Without this change, the "retire in order" handshake (next_to_retire++, broadcast, unlock) runs before the loop that waits for qp->users to drop to zero. That decouples the order-enforcement signal from the condition it's supposed to guarantee: a subsequent writer blocked on next_to_retire could be woken and proceed to retire its own (different) qp while the current writer's qp still has active readers. Once the QP ring holds more than the default 3 entries, this permits a qp to be freed/reused while still referenced by a reader, producing a use-after-free. The on-disk code avoids this by moving the increment/broadcast/unlock to after the reader-count busy-wait loop in both the pthread and Windows RCU implementations, so no writer is released to retire a qp until the current qp is verified to have zero readers.

findings.message: In ossl_synchronize_rcu(), the write-side retirement handshake (incrementing lock->next_to_retire, broadcasting lock->prior_signal, and unlocking lock->prior_lock) was reordered to happen BEFORE the loop that waits for the current qp's reader count (qp->users) to reach zero, instead of after it. The next_to_retire counter and its broadcast are the signal that tells the NEXT waiting writer (synchronizing on the following qp) that it may proceed to wait-for-readers and then retire/free its own qp. By publishing that signal before this writer has actually confirmed its own qp is reader-free, a second writer (and, once more than 3 QPs exist and the ring wraps, a third) can race ahead: it waits for its own qp's reader count, finds it already zero (because retire_qp()/reinitialization of a recycled qp slot can occur out of true order), and calls retire_qp() on a qp that an earlier, still-in-flight synchronize_rcu() call has not finished retiring, or is still mid-use. This produces a use-after-free / double-retire race on the rcu_qp structures. The bug only manifests when more than 3 QPs are configured (CRYPTO_THREAD_DEFAULT_QPS default is 3, so non-default configurations are required to trigger it), per the upstream description. The fix (commit 6e7be995fd7f) moves the next_to_retire increment/broadcast/unlock block to occur AFTER the reader-count-zero wait loop, ensuring a qp is only declared 'retired' to the next waiter once this writer has verified zero readers remain on it.
findings.suggestion: Move the next_to_retire increment, pthread_cond_broadcast(&lock->prior_signal), and pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock->prior_lock) block to occur AFTER the do/while loop that waits for qp->users (the reader count) to reach zero, so that the next writer is only released to proceed once this writer has verified its own qp has no remaining readers. Apply the equivalent reordering in crypto/threads_win.c for ossl_crypto_condvar_broadcast/ossl_crypto_mutex_unlock relative to the CRYPTO_atomic_load reader-count wait loop.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 9f85a036e331 on top of intro fff66adfc885 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): The log_frame() function returns 0 when ossl_quic_wire_peek_frame_header() fails without setting the *need_skip output parameter. The calling loop in log_frames() iterates while PACKET_remaining(&pkt) > 0, and relies on either (a) successful frame parsing which advances the packet position, or (b) need_skip being set to skip bytes. When peek_frame_header fails, neither condition is met: the packet position is not advanced and need_skip remains 0. This causes the loop to infinitely call log_frame() on the same packet position, resulting in an infinite loop that causes CI test failures and potential denial of service. Root cause: Missing error handling in log_frame() when peek_frame_header fails. The function returns failure (0) but does not set the need_skip output parameter, which the caller uses to determine how many bytes to skip. Without this, the caller loop never terminates because PACKET_remaining() continues to return a positive value.

Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): In ssl/statem/extensions.c, the final_maxfragmentlen() extension-processing callback was changed (while fixing PSK handling of the max_fragment_length extension) to unconditionally dereference s->session at the top of the function in order to initialize s->session->ext.max_fragment_len_mode when it is unspecified. However, the function retained a later guard 'if (s->session && USE_MAX_FRAGMENT_LENGTH_EXT(s->session))', implying the author was aware s->session could be NULL in this code path, yet the new dereference above it was left unguarded. Root cause: A new dereference of s->session was introduced above an existing NULL check for the same pointer, instead of placing the NULL check before any use of s->session. The refactor removed the old PSK-resumption-specific check (which happened to also reference s->session only after other guards) and replaced it with unconditional access, without re-validating that s->session could still be NULL at function entry in all call paths.

findings.message: final_maxfragmentlen() unconditionally dereferences s->session (via s->session->ext.max_fragment_len_mode) at the top of the function, before the existing NULL check 'if (s->session && USE_MAX_FRAGMENT_LENGTH_EXT(s->session))' further down. s->session can legitimately be NULL at this point in the handshake state machine (this extension-processing callback runs for both client and server, and in some PSK / early handshake states the session has not yet been established or resumed). This introduces a crash (NULL pointer dereference / DoS) reachable by a remote peer that drives the handshake into a state where final_maxfragmentlen() is invoked with s->session == NULL.
findings.suggestion: Move the NULL check for s->session to the very top of the function, before any dereference, and return early (success) if it is NULL, since there is nothing to do for max-fragment-length handling without a session.
findings.title: NULL pointer dereference of s->session in final_maxfragmentlen()

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 99ea6b38430d on top of intro 9a055c89170b via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The function ossl_quic_get_peer_token calls ossl_quic_build_new_token(peer, NULL, 0) to create a lookup key, but does not check if the returned key is NULL before using it in lh_QUIC_TOKEN_retrieve(). When the peer address hasn't been set on a QUIC channel yet (as happens early in connection establishment in the http3 demo), ossl_quic_build_new_token returns NULL because BIO_ADDR_rawaddress fails on the uninitialized peer. The NULL key is then passed to lh_QUIC_TOKEN_retrieve which dereferences it, causing a segmentation fault. Root cause: The ossl_quic_get_peer_token function was introduced without proper error handling for the case where ossl_quic_build_new_token returns NULL. The ossl_quic_build_new_token function returns NULL when BIO_ADDR_rawaddress fails on the peer parameter, which occurs when the peer address hasn't been set on the QUIC channel yet. The code proceeds to use this NULL key in lh_QUIC_TOKEN_retrieve without checking.
