agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c0527256d2e6 on top of intro 3d254b31344e via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): OSSL_DECODER_CTX_new_for_pkey() in crypto/encode_decode/decoder_pkey.c maintains a per-library-context cache of decoder chains, protected by cache->lock (a CRYPTO_RWLOCK). When no cached template exists, the function releases its read lock, builds a new decoder chain, then re-acquires the lock as a write lock in order to insert the new entry into the cache hashtable (lh_DECODER_CACHE_ENTRY_insert). Commit 3d254b31344e82b8f10fda8bab196757a377eb63 added error handling for the case where the hashtable insert itself fails (e.g. due to an internal allocation failure while the hashtable is resizing), routing that failure to a shared 'err:' cleanup label via 'goto err;'. That cleanup label frees the OSSL_DECODER_CTX and cache entry but does not release cache->lock, which had already been acquired for writing just before the insert. Consequently, whenever the hashtable insert fails, the function returns with the write lock still held. A later call into the same function (in the same thread, or any thread under a rwlock implementation that deadlocks on relocking) that attempts to acquire a read lock on cache->lock will fail/deadlock — this was observed as an assertion failure (EBUSY on CRYPTO_THREAD_read_lock) during OpenSSL's memory-failure injection testing. Root cause: A new error-handling branch (checking lh_DECODER_CACHE_ENTRY_error) was added that jumps into a shared 'err:' cleanup path, but that cleanup path was written for the earlier failure points in the function (all of which occur before the write lock is taken) and therefore does not release cache->lock. The developer who added the new error check overlooked that this particular 'goto err' occurs after the lock had already been acquired, unlike the other 'goto err' sites in the same function.

fix_commit_message:
Fix missing unlock in decoder_pkey.c

We hit an assertion failure during a call to CRYPTO_THREAD_read_lock
during memfail testing.

This was caused by us attempting to take a read lock in the same thread
that already held the same lock for writing resulting in an EBUSY
return.

Fix it by ensuring the lock is released in the error path.

commit_message:
Fix a leak in an error path in OSSL_DECODER_CTX_new_for_pkey()

Found via the reproducible error injection in #21668

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tom Cosgrove <tom.cosgrove@arm.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/21723)

findings.message: In OSSL_DECODER_CTX_new_for_pkey(), when constructing a new decoder cache entry, the code takes a write lock on cache->lock via CRYPTO_THREAD_write_lock() and then attempts to insert the new entry into the hashtable with lh_DECODER_CACHE_ENTRY_insert(). This commit added an explicit check of lh_DECODER_CACHE_ENTRY_error() after the insert to detect an allocation failure inside the hash table (e.g. out-of-memory while growing the table). On error it sets ctx = NULL, raises an error, and jumps to the 'err:' label via 'goto err;'. However, the 'err:' label only calls decoder_cache_entry_free(newcache) and OSSL_DECODER_CTX_free(ctx) before returning — it never calls CRYPTO_THREAD_unlock(cache->lock) to release the write lock that was just acquired a few lines above. As a result, on this specific out-of-memory/error path the function returns while still holding the write lock on cache->lock. Any subsequent call into OSSL_DECODER_CTX_new_for_pkey() (even from the same thread, e.g. under memory-failure/fuzz testing) that tries to take a read lock on the same cache->lock will either deadlock or, in debug/assert builds using pthread error-checking mutexes, hit an assertion failure (EBUSY) because the thread already holds the lock for writing. This is essentially a resource-leak/lock-leak bug that leads to a permanently corrupted lock state for the OSSL_LIB_CTX-scoped decoder cache.
findings.suggestion: Release the write lock on cache->lock before jumping to the error label, or make the 'err:' label unlock the lock only when it is known to be held (e.g. track a boolean, or restructure so the lock is always released along every path once acquired). The simplest fix, as later applied upstream, is to call CRYPTO_THREAD_unlock(cache->lock) immediately before the 'goto err;' in the lh_DECODER_CACHE_ENTRY_error() branch.
findings.title: Missing CRYPTO_THREAD_unlock on hashtable-insert error path in OSSL_DECODER_CTX_new_for_pkey()

findings.message: The OSSL_HASH ASN1 structure defines hashValue as an OPTIONAL field (ASN1_OPT(OSSL_HASH, hashValue, ASN1_BIT_STRING)). The i2r_HASH() print routine, used when rendering the attributeDescriptor X.509v3 extension (reachable from CRL/certificate extension printing), unconditionally dereferences hash->hashValue->data and hash->hashValue->length without first checking that hash->hashValue is non-NULL. Because hashValue is optional in the ASN.1 definition, a crafted certificate/CRL can omit it, causing hash->hashValue to be NULL when i2r_HASH is reached, leading to a NULL pointer dereference (crash) during extension printing (e.g. `openssl crl -text`, or any application that prints an untrusted CRL/cert containing this extension). This was discovered by OSS-Fuzz via the CRL fuzz target.
findings.suggestion: Before dereferencing hash->hashValue, check it for NULL and return an error (or skip printing the hash value) if it is NULL, since the ASN.1 definition marks hashValue as optional.
findings.title: NULL pointer dereference of optional hashValue in i2r_HASH

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 22417bc14d6b on top of intro 03ce37e11729 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): On riscv64, OpenSSL's ChaCha20_ctr32() dispatcher chooses a vectorized (RVV/Zbb/Zvkb) assembly implementation of ChaCha20 whenever the CPU advertises the relevant extensions and the input length exceeds one block, without verifying that the input and output buffer pointers are properly aligned. The vector assembly routines perform vector loads/stores that assume aligned memory; on real riscv64 hardware with the V extension enabled, unaligned `out`/`inp` pointers cause a crash (bus error / illegal instruction), even though the same code runs fine under QEMU emulation which is more permissive about misaligned vector accesses. Root cause: The feature-detection-based dispatch logic for selecting the RISC-V vector ChaCha20 implementation checked only CPU capability flags (RISCV_HAS_ZBB, riscv_vlen, RISCV_HAS_ZVKB) and input length, but never validated pointer alignment of the `out`/`inp` buffers before invoking vector load/store based assembly routines that require (or strongly prefer) aligned accesses on real hardware.
commit_message:
riscv: Provide a vector only implementation of Chacha20 cipher

Although we have a Zvkb version of Chacha20, the Zvkb from the RISC-V
Vector Cryptography Bit-manipulation extension was ratified in late 2023
and does not come to the RVA23 Profile. Many CPUs in 2024 currently do not
support Zvkb but may have Vector and Bit-manipulation, which are already in
the RVA22 Profile. This commit provides a vector-only implementation that
replaced the vror with vsll+vsrl+vor and can provide enough speed for

findings.message: ChaCha20_ctr32() on riscv64 selects the vector/Zbb (and optionally Zvkb) assembly implementations of ChaCha20 purely based on length and CPU feature flags (RISCV_HAS_ZBB(), riscv_vlen() >= 128, RISCV_HAS_ZVKB()). It never checks whether the `out` and `inp` buffer pointers are aligned to the machine word size. The RISC-V vector assembly routines (ChaCha20_ctr32_v_zbb / ChaCha20_ctr32_v_zbb_zvkb) use vector load/store instructions that, on real hardware with the Vector (V) extension enabled, can fault or crash on unaligned pointers even though it works fine under QEMU emulation. Since callers of ChaCha20_ctr32() (e.g. EVP cipher code) do not guarantee any particular alignment of input/output buffers, this leads to a crash (SIGBUS/SIGSEGV/illegal instruction depending on platform) whenever a caller passes unaligned buffers on real riscv64 V-extension hardware, i.e. a denial-of-service by user-controlled buffer alignment.
findings.suggestion: Add an alignment check for both the `out` and `inp` pointers to the dispatch condition, falling back to the portable C implementation (ChaCha20_ctr32_c) whenever either buffer is not aligned to sizeof(size_t), as done in the upstream fix.
findings.title: Missing pointer-alignment check before dispatching to RISC-V vector ChaCha20 routines

findings.message: The code added to ossl_x509_check_cert_time() (and mirrored in ossl_x509_check_certificate_times) treats the raw data buffer returned by ASN1_STRING_get0_data() on the certificate's notAfter field as a NUL-terminated C string and passes it to strcmp() to compare against the literal "99991231235959Z". ASN1_STRING objects are NOT guaranteed to be NUL-terminated and their length is tracked explicitly via the ASN1_STRING.length field, not by a terminating NUL byte. An attacker-supplied (or malformed) certificate can craft a notAfter ASN1_TIME whose underlying buffer is shorter than 15 bytes and does not contain a NUL terminator within the allocated buffer, causing strcmp() to read past the end of the heap allocation while searching for a terminator that never appears within bounds. This results in a heap-buffer-overflow (out-of-bounds read), which was discovered via OSS-Fuzz/CI fuzzing of certificate parsing and verification.
findings.suggestion: Do not treat ASN1_STRING data as a NUL-terminated C string. Explicitly check the ASN1_STRING length equals the expected literal length (15 for "99991231235959Z") before comparing, and use memcmp() instead of strcmp() to compare exactly that many bytes.
findings.title: Heap-buffer-overflow via strcmp() on non-NUL-terminated ASN1_STRING data in ossl_x509_check_cert_time

findings.message: When BIO_sendmmsg() and BIO_recvmmsg() invoke the BIO_CB_*MMSG|BIO_CB_RETURN callback via bio_call_callback(), they pass a hard-coded NULL for the `processed` output parameter, while passing the actual number of processed messages (`ret`) as the `inret` argument. Prior to this commit, `inret` was always hard-coded to 0 for the RETURN callback, so the legacy-callback branch in bio_call_callback() (`if (inret > 0 && (oper & BIO_CB_RETURN) ...) { if (*processed > INT_MAX) ... inret = *processed; }`) could never execute, since inret was never >0. This commit changed the call so that `inret` is now the real `ret` value returned by the underlying bsendmmsg/brecvmmsg method, which can legitimately be >0 whenever any messages were sent/received. When a legacy (non-_ex) BIO callback is installed on the BIO via BIO_set_callback(), and BIO_sendmmsg()/BIO_recvmmsg() successfully process at least one message, bio_call_callback() will now dereference the `processed` pointer (`*processed > INT_MAX`) even though NULL was passed for it, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (reported by Stanislav Fort, Aisle Research).
findings.suggestion: Pass the actual `msgs_processed` pointer (instead of NULL) as the `processed` argument to bio_call_callback() for the BIO_CB_SENDMMSG|BIO_CB_RETURN and BIO_CB_RECVMMSG|BIO_CB_RETURN calls, so that the legacy-callback compatibility path in bio_call_callback() can safely write/read through it whenever inret (the return value) is greater than zero.

agent_reasoning: The bug was that `evp_Encode_Ctx_st.length` was mutable and set to 0 by `EVP_DecodeInit`. The encoding functions (`evp_encodeblock_int`, `EVP_EncodeUpdate`) used `ctx->length` as a modulo/divisor. If encode operations were invoked on a context that had been through `EVP_DecodeInit` (e.g., via BIO's b64_ctrl calling EVP_EncodeFinal), `ctx->length` would be 0 and the `%` operations would trigger a division-by-zero (SIGFPE). The fix eliminates the mutable field entirely, replacing it with the compile-time constant `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH 48`. Since the constant is never zero, the divide-by-zero cannot occur. The on-disk code implements this safe design from the start, so no decoder-initialized context can ever supply a zero divisor to the encoder paths.

intro_commit_message:
Added AVX2 encoding + scalar improvements

Reviewed-by: Dmitry Belyavskiy <beldmit@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <paul.dale@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/29178)
pr_description:
The `evp_Encode_Ctx_st` struct carried an `int length` field that was set to 48 during encoding initialization and 0 during decoding initialization, but was never changed at any point during operation. Because the value is invariant, keeping it as a mutable struct field is unnecessary and creates a footgun: any code path that obtains an `EVP_ENCODE_CTX` initialized for *decoding* (where `length` was set to 0) can accidentally invoke the encoding functions, which use `ctx->length` as a divisor — resulting in a division-by-zero fault.

This PR removes `int length` from `evp_Encode_Ctx_st` entirely and introduces a compile-time constant `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH 48` in `evp_local.h`. All sites in `encode.c` and `enc_b64_scalar.c` that previously read `ctx->length` for encoding decisions now reference this constant directly.

Changes:
- `crypto/evp/evp_local.h`: Add `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH` macro; remove the `length` field and its comment from `evp_Encode_Ctx_st`.
- `crypto/evp/encode.c`: Add `#include <assert.h>`; replace `OPENSSL_assert(ctx->length …)` with `assert(EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH …)`; replace all `ctx->length` references in `EVP_EncodeUpdate` with `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH`; remove the now-meaningless `ctx->length = 48` assignment from `EVP_EncodeInit` and `ctx->length = 0` from `EVP_DecodeInit`.
- `crypto/evp/enc_b64_scalar.c`: Replace every `ctx->length` usage in `evp_encodeblock_int` with `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH`.

The `EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH` value (48) is divisible by 3, which is a requirement for the AVX2-optimized code path and is documented in the macro comment.
pr_title: base64 encoder: Make ctx->length a constant (EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH)

findings.message: The evp_encodeblock_int function performs modulo operations using ctx->length without validating that it is non-zero. When EVP_DecodeInit is called, it sets ctx->length = 0. If encode functions are later invoked with such a context (e.g., through EVP_EncodeFinal called via BIO_ctrl), the modulo operation '% ctx->length' causes a division by zero (FPE). This was discovered by oss-fuzz through the SMIME fuzzer.
findings.suggestion: Replace all uses of ctx->length with a compile-time constant EVP_ENCODE_B64_LENGTH (which equals 48) since ctx->length is never modified after initialization. This eliminates the possibility of division by zero since the constant is always non-zero.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f3dbf6aa79c3 on top of intro 0152e4f9f750 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The CCS buffering mechanism for UDP reorder tolerance does not account for trailing data in the current record buffer. When an early-arriving CCS is buffered using `has_change_cipher_spec = 1` and `goto redo`, the code continues processing. Later, when the buffered CCS is delivered (when `dtls_ccs_expected()` returns true), it triggers `tls_process_change_cipher_spec()` -> `ssl3_do_change_cipher_spec()` -> `tls1_change_cipher_state()` -> `ssl_set_new_record_layer()`, which frees the old record layer buffer via `dtls_free()` -> `tls_free()` -> `tls_int_free()` -> `ossl_tls_buffer_release()`. However, if there is trailing data left in the current record at the point of the cipher change, the pointers to that buffer become dangling. Subsequent reads via `dtls1_read_bytes()` access freed memory, causing a heap-use-after-free. Root cause: The CCS buffering mechanism using `has_change_cipher_spec = 1` and `goto redo` does not verify that all data in the current record buffer has been consumed before allowing a cipher state change. When the buffered CCS triggers ssl_set_new_record_layer(), the old buffer is freed, but dangling pointers to trailing data in that buffer remain, leading to use-after-free on subsequent reads.

fix_commit_message:
Fix a Use-After-Free bug in the DTLS code

The newly added #30225 introduced a UAF bug in the master branch found
by the dtlsserver fuzzer. If a CCS arrives early and there is trailing
data left in the current record at the point that we change epoch then
the buffer holding the trailing data is freed as part of setting up the
new record layer, but we still have dangling references into that buffer
causing the UAF.

Fixes #30487
